subtle

/SUT-ul/ — the 'b' is silent; rhymes with 'shuttle' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Subtle is so slight or delicate that it is difficult to detect.

The perfume left only a subtle trace of jasmine in the hallway.

Example

The art expert stared at the two identical-looking paintings for an hour. Finally she pointed to a single brushstroke in the corner, thinner than an eyelash, that the forger had angled the wrong way.

The difference was subtle — so slight it was difficult to detect. An 'obvious' flaw jumps out at anyone; a subtle one reveals itself only to careful, trained attention.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

faint: Faint means barely perceptible — a faint sound or glow sits at the very edge of the senses, yet you do notice it. Subtle is about the care detection demands: a subtle difference may not be weak at all, but only close attention reveals it.

understated: Understated means presented quietly and without show — an intentional choice to keep something low-key. Subtle describes how hard a thing is to detect, whether or not anyone chose that. An understated dress is modest on purpose; a subtle flaw simply hides.

slight: Slight measures size: a slight change or a slight delay is small in degree, however easy it may be to see. Subtle measures detectability instead — a subtle clue can matter greatly, yet it is so delicate that it is easily missed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

obvious: easy to see or understand

glaring: impossible to miss, often unpleasantly so

Where it sits · how easily it escapes notice — muted → subtle → imperceptible

muted vs. subtle: Muted is weaker than subtle — something muted is toned down but still plainly there, while something subtle takes real attention to detect at all.

imperceptible vs. subtle: Imperceptible is stronger than subtle — a subtle detail is hard to detect, but an imperceptible one cannot be detected by the senses at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — sub-

Prefix — sub-: under (Latin)

Root — tle

Root — tle: web, fine woven thread (from Latin tela; subtilis, 'fine as thread passing under the web of a loom,' wore down through Old French soutil to -tle)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin subtilis likely described thread fine enough to pass 'under the web' of a loom: sub- ('under') + tle (worn down from tela, 'web, fine woven thread'). A subtle thing is woven that finely: present, but hard to detect.

Where This Word Comes From

Where This Word Comes From: Latin tela ('a fine-woven web') built no other common English word by itself, but it comes from a deeper root that built plenty: texere, 'to weave,' behind text, texture, and textile. A text is literally 'woven' words. Something subtle is woven so finely you can barely see the threads.
